steps.name: Sun only
steps.line: Sun only: we calculate the Sun positions at intervals of 1 minute, over a flat horizon. An independent recount differs by 0.065 hours a year or less. JPL Horizons differs by a median of 0.11 percent.

steps.name: snow-free ground
steps.line: Snow-free ground: 740 IMS satellite snow maps (daily, 4 km), from October 2015 to September 2025. We compared them with 139 weather stations.

steps.name: after terrain
steps.line: After terrain: the horizon of each area comes from Copernicus DEM GLO-90 elevation data, read on a 60 m grid.

steps.name: typical cloud
steps.line: Typical cloud: the monthly mean cloud from NASA POWER (CERES SYN1deg), 2001 to 2025, on a 1-degree grid of approximately 111 km.

rests_on.cloud_source: NASA POWER, POWER Climatology API v2.10.1, regional endpoint; data source named by the service: SYN1DEG (CERES SYN1deg)

line: Sun: our own positions, checked against JPL Horizons. Snow: IMS satellite maps, checked at 139 weather stations. Hills: Copernicus DEM GLO-90 elevation data. Cloud: monthly means from NASA POWER.

assumptions.text: An area is a square of approximately 11 km. One figure gives the value for all of the area.
Cloud is a monthly mean over all hours of day and night. It is not the chance that you can see a low Sun.
Snow on Antarctic rock is not measured. Thus, in Antarctica we count only the rock season, from 27 November to 1 March.
We count only spells of at least 2 hours. This is our choice, not an agency rule.
The snow-free odds are typical values for each ten-day period from October 2015 to September 2025. They are not a forecast for one year.
The Sun heights include the usual effect of the air on the direction of light (standard refraction).
